title: Fractions with rotis
subject: Maths
summary: Groups share three newspaper rotis, build their own fraction kits, then play into comparing fractions.
about: A compressed fractions unit that starts with real sharing. Table groups divide three newspaper rotis among themselves, draw their own 12 cm fraction kits, and play their way into comparing and equivalent fractions through Fraction War and an outdoor game.
in_my_classroom: Groups of four split three rotis more easily than groups of five, but every group finished. We made a wall picture of three rotis shared among four. Most students can now say which of two unit fractions is bigger.
what_id_change: Many students can't yet divide (11 ÷ 4), so word problems now always divide evenly. The concept carries the difficulty, not the arithmetic.

title: Angles as turns
subject: Maths
summary: Five days of making angles by hand: a paper fan, a folded square-paper angle tool, and turning clock hands.
about: Students make angles with their hands before naming them: the paper fan from the textbook (p. 34), an angle tool folded from square paper cut from A4, and clock hands turning 0, 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes. Day 5 moves to direction and real turns.
in_my_classroom: Students already knew clockwise and anticlockwise, so Day 5 got harder: a multi-step turns example, a tougher exit ticket and an extension reasoning question.

title: Keep Trying: The Chewing Gum Story
subject: English
summary: An original passage for teaching inference: “I think ___ because the text says ___.”
about: An original passage about how chewing gum came about, written to teach one skill: using evidence from the text to infer why people acted the way they did. The Big Question: why does trying new things matter, even when we're not sure it'll work?
in_my_classroom: We couldn't get through the whole passage in one period. I had first framed the story as a happy accident, then changed it to persistence, because the text shows people trying again and again.
what_id_change: Teacher read-aloud instead of echo reading. The core is Do Now, reading and modelled inference in about 35 minutes. Vocabulary and the written response move to homework.

title: The Rainbow
subject: English
summary: Christina Rossetti's poem over three days: meaning, word play, recitation, grammar and colour mixing.
about: Day 1 covers the poem and comprehension. Day 2 is word play: anagrams, a spin-wheel, rhyming and a three-voice recitation. Day 3 brings compound words, a journey paragraph, nouns and verbs, and colour mixing.

title: Community
subject: EVS
summary: Rural, urban and tribal communities, a food-chain activity on how we depend on each other, and help during disasters.
about: Day 1 covers what makes a community. Days 2 to 4 cover rural, urban and tribal life. Day 5 brings a food-chain activity on interdependence, other kinds of community, and how communities help during natural disasters.
what_id_change: Slides need big text and short, visual phrases. My first decks read like pasted notes.

title: Family
subject: EVS
summary: Family trees, relationships, joint and nuclear families, and a neighbourhood household survey.
about: Family tree symbols, naming relationships, joint and nuclear families, and how neighbours help each other, ending with a household survey of the neighbourhood.

title: Our Food, Our Health
subject: EVS
summary: A seven-day food diary and a Kitchen Detective task where students read a real nutrition label at home.
about: Given before the holiday break so students arrive at the nutrition unit with their own data. They keep a seven-day food diary and choose one task, such as Kitchen Detective, where they read a real nutrition label at home.

title: The Crew
subject: Classroom culture
summary: Captain and Crew roles, a 0–4 voice-level scale, a daily Do Now, and a restorative path for conflict.
about: A shared way of running the room: Captain and Crew roles, a 0–4 voice-level scale, a Do Now on the board every lesson, and a restorative path for conflict: Harbour, What Happened, Back on Deck, Ship's Log. “We are a crew. We sail together, we look after our own, and we make this a room where everyone can think, learn, and feel safe.”
what_id_change: Use the sea theme only where it does real work. Children tire of it when it leaks into every lesson.
